01-physical-theories: Experimental data alone cannot uniquely fix the mathematical axioms of a physical theory without operational principles that specify how preparations, transformations, and measurements compose.
In an operational framework, a physical system is characterized by the laboratory procedures that prepare it, act on it, and produce outcome probabilities.
Reconstructing quantum mechanics from operational axioms reveals which features of Hilbert space come from general probability rules and which come from distinctly quantum postulates.
02-states: An operational state is completely defined by the list of outcome probabilities it assigns to every possible measurement on the system.
Statistical mixing of preparations makes the state space a convex set whose extremal points are the pure states.
A finite set of fiducial measurements suffices to determine the state vector \(\mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^K\), and transformations act linearly on this state space to preserve convex mixtures.
03-effects: Each measurement outcome corresponds to a linear functional—an effect \(e\)—mapping every normalized state \(\omega\) to a probability \(e(\omega) \in [0,1]\).
The information capacity \(N\) of a system is the maximum number of states that can be distinguished from one another in a single-shot measurement.
Generalized probabilistic theories (GPTs) include classical probability, quantum theory, and hypothetical foil theories such as boxworld within a single geometric framework.
04-composition: No-signaling requires that marginal outcome probabilities on system \(A\) be independent of the measurement choice made on adistant system \(B\).
Local tomography postulates that the joint state of a composite system \(AB\) is completely determined by the statistics of product measurements \(e_A \otimes f_B\), so \(K_{AB} = K_A K_B\).
Even under local tomography and no-signaling, composite state spaces can contain non-product entangled states that correlate local outcomes more strongly than any shared classical randomness.
05-classical-theory: A classical system with \(N\) distinguishable outcomes has a state space that is a simplex with \(N\) vertices and \(K = N\) degrees of freedom.
Every mixed state in a classical simplex has a unique decomposition into pure vertices, leaving no room for interference or complementary measurements.
The reversible transformations of a classical simplex form the finite permutation group \(S_N\), so one pure state cannot be continuously and reversibly deformed into another.
06-continuous-reversibility: Postulating that every pure state can be transformed into any other along a continuous path of reversible operations rules out the discrete classical simplex.
Continuous reversibility between two distinguishable states forces intrinsic randomness: intermediate pure states must yield probabilistic outcomes when measured in the original basis.
For the simplest non-trivial system (\(N = 2\)), continuous reversibility requires the state space to be a Euclidean ball \(B^{K-1}\) of some dimension \(d = K - 1\).
07-the-qubit: Combining continuous reversibility, local tomography (\(K_{AB} = K_A K_B\)), and composite gate existence selects the three-dimensional Bloch ball (\(d = 3, K = 4\)) over all other Euclidean spheres.

Points in the Bloch ball \(\mathbf{r} \in B^3\) correspond one-to-one with \(2\times 2\) Hermitian density matrices \(\rho = \frac{1}{2}(I + \mathbf{r}\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma})\) over the complex numbers.
The trace rule \(P(k) = \mathrm{Tr}(E_k \rho)\) emerges naturally as the inner product between state vectors and effect vectors on the Bloch sphere.
08-larger-systems: Subspace equivalence states that any two systems or subspaces with the same number of distinguishable states \(N\) are operationally isomorphic.

Requiring every two-outcome subspace of an \(N\)-level system to form a three-dimensional Bloch ball forces the full state space to be the set of positive trace-one operators on \(\mathbb{C}^N\) with \(K = N^2\).
Every valid measurement on \(\mathbb{C}^N\) is represented by a positive operator-valued measure (POVM) \(\{E_k\}\) satisfying \(E_k \ge 0\) and \(\sum_k E_k = I\).
09-symmetry-and-dynamics: Wigner’s theorem establishes that any symmetry preserving transition probabilities \(|\langle\psi|\phi\rangle|^2\) on complex Hilbert space is implemented by a unitary or antiunitary operator.
A continuous one-parameter group of reversible time translations \(U(t+s) = U(t)U(s)\) must consist of unitary operators connected to the identity.
By Stone’s theorem, every continuous unitary group has a self-adjoint generator \(H\) such that \(U(t) = e^{-iHt/\hbar}\), yielding the time-dependent Schrödinger equation.
10-observables: A real-valued physical quantity whose outcomes have sharp repeatable eigenstates is represented by a self-adjoint operator \(A = \sum_a a\,P_a\) via the spectral theorem.
Two projective observables can be measured jointly without mutual disturbance if and only if their operators commute, \([A, B] = 0\).
Non-commuting observables obey the Robertson uncertainty relation \(\Delta A\,\Delta B \ge \frac{1}{2}|\langle[A,B]\rangle|\), reflecting the geometry of non-orthogonal state subspaces.
11-state-update: A quantum instrument describes both the outcome probability \(P(k) = \mathrm{Tr}(\mathcal{I}_k(\rho))\) and the normalized post-measurement state \(\rho_k = \mathcal{I}_k(\rho)/P(k)\).
For repeatable, minimally disturbing projective measurements, the state updates by the Lüders rule \(\rho \mapsto P_k \rho P_k / \mathrm{Tr}(P_k \rho)\).
In quantum theory, extracting information to distinguish non-orthogonal states inevitably disturbs at least one of them.
12-contextuality: A noncontextual hidden-variable model assigns pre-existing outcome values to observables independently of which compatible partner observables are measured alongside them.

Gleason’s theorem proves that in Hilbert spaces of dimension \(d \ge 3\), any frame function assigning additive probabilities to orthogonal projectors must have the Born-rule form \(\mathrm{Tr}(\rho P)\).
The Kochen–Specker and Peres–Mermin constructions exhibit finite sets of observables for which no noncontextual value assignment can satisfy all functional identities simultaneously.
13-entanglement: When a composite system is in an entangled pure state \(|\Psi\rangle_{AB}\), its subsystems do not possess pure states of their own and are described by mixed reduced density matrices \(\rho_A = \mathrm{Tr}_B(|\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi|)\).
Bell’s theorem shows that local hidden-variable models obey the CHSH inequality \(|S| \le 2\), whereas entangled quantum states reach Tsirelson’s bound \(2\sqrt{2}\).
Quantum nonlocality violates local causality in outcome correlations while strictly respecting operational no-signaling.
14-identical-particles: When two particles are operationally indistinguishable, swapping them leaves every observable expectation value invariant, so physical states lie in representations of the permutation group.

In three spatial dimensions, topological equivalence of double exchanges restricts identical particles to symmetric bosonic states (\(P_{12}|\Psi\rangle = +|\Psi\rangle\)) or antisymmetric fermionic states (\(P_{12}|\Psi\rangle = -|\Psi\rangle\)).
The Pauli exclusion principle follows directly from antisymmetrization, while two-dimensional systems allow braided anyonic phases \(e^{i\theta}\).
15-open-systems: Every mixed state \(\rho_A\) arises as the marginal of a pure entangled state \(|\Psi\rangle_{AE}\) on a larger composite system, unique up to unitary transformations on the purifying environment \(E\).

Stinespring’s dilation theorem proves that any completely positive trace-preserving (CPTP) quantum channel \(\mathcal{E}(\rho) = \sum_k K_k \rho K_k^\dagger\) is equivalent to unitary interaction with an environment followed by partial trace.
Decoherence suppresses off-diagonal interference terms in the pointer basis selected by system–environment interactions, producing apparent classical mixtures locally.
16-infinite-dimensions: Canonical commutation relations \([X, P] = i\hbar I\) cannot be realized by finite-dimensional matrices because the trace of a finite commutator always vanishes.

In infinite-dimensional separable Hilbert space \(L^2(\mathbb{R})\), unbounded observables like position and momentum require careful domain definitions and projection-valued measures over continuous spectra.
The Stone–von Neumann theorem guarantees that all irreducible unitary representations of the Weyl commutation relations are unitarily equivalent to Schrödinger wave mechanics.
17-assumptions-and-alternatives: Five operational principles—causality, local tomography, subspace equivalence, continuous reversibility, and purification—uniquely single out finite-dimensional complex quantum theory.

Relaxing local tomography yields real-amplitude quantum mechanics (where \(K_{AB} > K_A K_B\)), while relaxing continuous reversibility or subspace equivalence leads to classical or post-quantum foil theories.
Open foundational frontiers include reconstructing quantum field theory and understanding how causal structure behaves when spacetime geometry itself is in quantum superposition.
